title: What PMs Actually Do
mentor_message: Day 1. Most people start PM prep by watching YouTube videos and reading listicles. You're going to skip all of that. In the next 90 minutes you'll understand why the PM role exists - not just what it involves. Open the learn block now.

learn.concept: PM role vs myths, PM is not project manager, not mini-CEO, the value of saying no, PM as the person who defines what to build and why, India context with CRED/Zepto examples
learn.body:
What does a Product Manager actually do? The tech industry is full of myths: PMs are 'mini-CEOs', or they are just project managers who schedule meetings, or they are designers who can't draw. None of this is true.

In reality, a PM is responsible for deciding *what* to build and *why* to build it, while engineering decides *how* to build it. A PM acts as the bridge between user needs, business goals, and engineering constraints. At companies like Zepto, a PM doesn't write code or design the UI, but they frame the problem: how can we reduce order packing time at dark stores from 2 minutes to 60 seconds? At CRED, a PM works on the retention loop: how do we make credit card bill payments engaging enough that users open the app daily?

The most important and underappreciated PM skill is the ability to say 'no'. You will have 100 feature requests from sales, founders, and users. If you build them all, you get a bloated, unusable product. Your job is to prioritize ruthlessly based on evidence and impact.

title: User Research and Jobs to be Done
mentor_message: Day 2. JTBD is one of those frameworks that sounds obvious and is harder to apply than it looks. Most candidates say 'users want convenience' and leave it there. By the end of today, you'll have 5 JTBD statements that actually reveal something. Start the clock.

learn.concept: Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework, outcome vs feature thinking, Kano model basics, how to design user research questions
learn.body:
To build products users love, you must understand their underlying motivations. The Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework states that customers don't buy products; they 'hire' them to do a job. As Clayton Christensen famously said, people don't want a quarter-inch drill; they want a quarter-inch hole.

For example, why do users use Swiggy? To get food. But the 'job' varies. One user hires Swiggy because they are working late and need quick fuel (Job 1: Convenience). Another user hires Swiggy Gourmet because they are hosting a dinner party and want to impress guests (Job 2: Social status). The features needed for these two jobs are completely different.

When designing user research, avoid asking: 'Would you use a feature that does X?' Users will say yes, but they won't pay for it. Instead, ask about their past behavior: 'Tell me about the last time you ordered food for a group. How did you do it? What was frustrating?' Focus on outcomes, not solutions.
learn.resource_label: HBR — Know Your Customers' Jobs to be Done

quiz.question: What is the difference between a feature and a job in the JTBD framework?
quiz.rubric_hint: A feature is the solution/mechanism. A job is the progress or outcome the user is trying to achieve.

quiz.question: Why is asking users 'what features do you want' a bad user research practice?
quiz.rubric_hint: Users are bad at inventing solutions but good at describing pain points. They will suggest features they won't actually use.

practice.question: Tell me about a problem you solved - walk me through how you identified the real problem vs. the surface complaint.

title: Problem Framing
mentor_message: Day 3. The most common PM interview mistake is proposing solutions before the problem is clear. Today's practice forces you to stop before solutions. Start the clock.

learn.concept: Root cause vs symptom, 5 Whys technique, problem statement structure that doesn't contain the solution, Indian fintech/quick commerce examples
learn.body:
If you define a problem poorly, your solution will fail. A common trap is writing a problem statement like: 'Users need a WhatsApp chatbot.' This is a solution, not a problem. A real problem statement defines the user, the context, the pain point, and the impact, without hinting at the technology.

To find the root cause of a problem, use the 5 Whys technique. For example:
1. Why is Swiggy Instamart's average order value down?
- Because users are ordering fewer items.
2. Why are they ordering fewer items?
- Because they only buy essentials like milk and bread.
3. Why do they only buy essentials?
- Because they are afraid other items will be out of stock or of poor quality.
4. Why do they believe that?
- Because they had a bad experience with fresh produce in the past.
5. Why did they have a bad experience?
- Because our inventory quality check at dark store X failed.

Now, the problem is not 'average order value is down' — it is 'users do not trust dark store quality check, leading to restricted cart sizes.' The solutions for this (better QC transparency, quality guarantees) are completely different from just sending discounts to increase order value.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't a problem statement contain the solution?
quiz.rubric_hint: Including the solution limits creativity and prevents you from exploring alternative, potentially better ways to solve the user's core pain point.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a symptom and a root cause?
quiz.rubric_hint: A symptom is the visible output/metric drop (e.g. drop in retention). A root cause is the underlying behavior or technical failure driving that drop.

voice.prompt: How do you know when you've found the real problem versus a symptom?

title: Metrics and Success Criteria
mentor_message: Day 4. Metrics questions appear in every PM interview. The trap is picking a metric that sounds smart without justifying it. Today you'll practice the justification. Start the clock.

learn.concept: AARRR funnel, DAU/WAU/MAU, engagement vs retention vs revenue metrics, leading vs lagging indicators, how to define success before building
learn.body:
Metrics are how a PM measures whether their product is succeeding. The most common framework is the AARRR funnel:
1. Acquisition: How do users find us? (e.g. app downloads)
2. Activation: Do they have a good first experience? (e.g. first completed UPI transaction on PhonePe)
3. Retention: Do they come back? (e.g. D30 retention)
4. Referral: Do they tell others? (e.g. promo code shares)
5. Revenue: How do we monetize? (e.g. average order value)

As a PM, you must distinguish between leading and lagging indicators. A lagging indicator (like revenue) tells you what happened in the past. A leading indicator (like user signup completions or weekly active usage) predicts future success.

Another critical distinction is engagement vs retention. Engagement is how much time or actions a user takes (DAU/MAU ratio). Retention is whether they return. A product can have high engagement initially (due to novelty) but terrible retention. You must define success criteria *before* launching a feature so you don't shift the goalposts later.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a leading indicator and a lagging indicator?
quiz.rubric_hint: Leading indicators are predictive and actionable (e.g., signups). Lagging indicators are output-oriented and historical (e.g., monthly revenue).

quiz.question: Why is high engagement not a guarantee of high retention?
quiz.rubric_hint: Users can use a product intensively for a short period (high engagement) but completely abandon it later (poor retention).

title: North Star Metric
mentor_message: Day 5. Everyone has heard of North Star metrics. Almost nobody can explain why the wrong North Star destroys a company. Today that changes. Start the clock.

learn.concept: North Star vs counter metrics, Goodhart's Law, why optimizing the wrong metric kills products, examples from Paytm MAU vs transaction value, Swiggy orders vs order value
learn.body:
A North Star Metric is the single key metric that best captures the core value your product delivers to its customers. It should align customer value, product strategy, and business growth.

For example, Airbnb's North Star is 'nights booked' — not app downloads or active users. Nights booked captures value for both guests (finding a place to stay) and hosts (making money), which drives Airbnb's business growth.

However, a North Star can be dangerous if optimized blindly. This is Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' If Swiggy's PM only optimizes for 'number of orders', the team might run heavy discount campaigns that bring low-value orders, destroying unit economics. To prevent this, every North Star must have a 'counter metric'. If your North Star is 'number of orders', your counter metric should be 'average order margin' or 'customer satisfaction rate'. Together, they keep the product healthy.
learn.resource_label: Amplitude — North Star Playbook

quiz.question: What is Goodhart's Law in the context of product metrics?
quiz.rubric_hint: Goodhart's Law states that once a metric becomes the target, people will game the system to hit it, often destroying the original value.

quiz.question: Why does a North Star metric need a counter metric?
quiz.rubric_hint: A counter metric acts as a guardrail to ensure the North Star is not optimized at the expense of business health or user experience.

title: Prioritization Frameworks
mentor_message: Day 6. Prioritization is where PMs earn their salary. The trap is picking a framework and refusing to deviate from it. Today you'll see that the framework is just the starting point. Start the clock.

learn.concept: RICE (Reach Impact Confidence Effort), ICE, MoSCoW, opportunity scoring, when each framework fits which context, how to handle stakeholder disagreements
learn.body:
PMs don't suffer from a lack of ideas; they suffer from too many. Prioritization is the process of deciding what is most important to build *now*.

The most popular quantitative framework is RICE:
- Reach: How many users will this impact in a given timeframe? (e.g. 50,000 users/month)
- Impact: How much will this improve their experience? (scored 3 for massive, 2 for high, 1 for medium, 0.5 for low)
- Confidence: How sure are we of our estimates? (100% for high, 80% for medium, 50% for low)
- Effort: How much engineering time will this take? (measured in person-months, e.g., 3 developer months)

Score = (Reach * Impact * Confidence) / Effort

While RICE is great for mature products, early-stage startups often use ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease) because it is faster and requires less historical data. The trap is thinking prioritization is pure math. Frameworks are tools to structure conversation and expose assumptions — not to make the final decision. You must still use strategic judgment to align choices with company goals.
learn.resource_label: Intercom — RICE Prioritization

quiz.question: Under what circumstances would you use ICE instead of RICE?
quiz.rubric_hint: Use ICE at early-stage startups or for rapid prototyping when Reach is hard to estimate and speed is more important than precision.

quiz.question: What is the primary danger of relying purely on a mathematical score for prioritization?
quiz.rubric_hint: It can be gamed by inflating impact/confidence numbers, and it ignores strategic alignment or developer dependencies.

title: Writing a PRD
mentor_message: Day 7. A PRD is not documentation. It's a decision record. Today you'll write one that actually makes decisions. Start the clock.

learn.concept: PRD structure (problem, success metrics, user stories, scope, open questions), what goes in vs what stays out, how PRDs differ at startups vs large companies
learn.body:
A Product Requirements Document (PRD) is the source of truth for a feature. It aligns design, engineering, and business on what is being built. A common mistake is writing a 40-page PRD that nobody reads. A great PRD is concise, focused, and decisions-driven.

A standard PRD structure includes:
1. Objective: What problem are we solving? (The 'Why')
2. Success Metrics: How will we know we solved it?
3. User Stories & Requirements: What is the user experience? (e.g. 'As a user, I want to filter transaction history by date so I can find a specific receipt quickly.')
4. Out of Scope: What are we *not* building in V1? (Crucial for avoiding scope creep)
5. Open Questions: Risks or decisions still to be made.

At a startup, PRDs are short and updated frequently. In larger companies, they are more detailed to coordinate across multiple teams. Regardless of company size, the PM's goal in writing a PRD is to drive clarity and alignment, not just to document steps.

quiz.question: Why is the 'Out of Scope' section crucial in a PRD?
quiz.rubric_hint: It prevents scope creep by explicitly aligning stakeholders on what features are postponed for future iterations.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a user story and a functional requirement?
quiz.rubric_hint: A user story describes the user value and motivation. A functional requirement specifies how the system behaves to enable that value.

title: Boss Challenge: Full Product Teardown
mentor_message: Day 8. One week in. Most people have some theory now but haven't tested it. Today finds out. A teardown is not a summary - it is a judgment. You are on record. 90 minutes. Go.

learn.concept: Combining Days 1-7 — a product teardown is not a feature list, it's a judgment call
learn.body:
Congratulations on completing Week 1. Today is your first Boss Challenge: a full product teardown of an Indian consumer app. A teardown is not a walkthrough or a summary of features. It is a critical audit of a product's strategy, user experience, and roadmap.

A great teardown answers:
1. Who is the target user and what is their primary JTBD?
2. What is the core retention loop of the product?
3. What friction exists in the core funnel (e.g. signup, checkout)?
4. What strategic choices did the team make that succeeded, and what failed?
5. What is the next major feature they should build, backed by evidence?

You will choose CRED, Zepto, or Groww and spend the next 90 minutes performing a deep teardown. You are expected to criticize feature choices and propose additions based on product principles, not personal preferences.
learn.resource_label: Lenny's Newsletter — The Product Teardown

quiz.question: What is the single biggest difference between a product review and a product teardown?
quiz.rubric_hint: A review evaluates usability from a user's perspective. A teardown evaluates strategic decisions, metrics, and business viability from a PM's perspective.

quiz.question: How do you identify a product's core retention loop from the outside?
quiz.rubric_hint: By observing what actions/triggers bring a user back repeatedly, and what investment they make (data, money, network) that makes leaving hard.

voice.prompt: Present your teardown out loud as if you are in an interview. Hit all the key points in under 8 minutes.

title: APIs for PMs
mentor_message: Day 9. Most candidates skip this concept because it seems technical or boring. You won't. Today you will learn REST anatomy and practice it under time constraint. Start the timer.

learn.body:
Welcome to Day 9 of the PM Accelerator. Today we are focusing on APIs for PMs, which is a critical part of the Technical PM Lens phase.

In product management, REST anatomy, endpoints, methods, rate limits, webhooks vs polling, PM buy vs build decisions. Understanding this is vital because it directly impacts your ability to make decisions and align stakeholders. For example, at leading Indian companies like CRED, Groww, and Razorpay, PMs grapple with these issues daily. CRED uses these concepts to design premium financial services, Swiggy uses them to optimize logistics and routing efficiency, and Zepto applies them to manage inventory in real time across hundreds of dark stores.

When thinking about APIs for PMs, you should always structure your approach. First, identify the core user and their jobs-to-be-done. Second, measure the current performance using leading and lagging indicators. Third, evaluate the engineering effort against the potential business impact. And finally, design a rollout strategy that minimizes risk while maximizing learning.

In interviews, you will frequently face questions that test your depth in APIs for PMs. They want to see if you can think from first principles, evaluate tradeoffs, and make a firm recommendation. Avoid generic answers like 'we will make it user-friendly' or 'we will use AI' without explaining the mechanism. Instead, be concrete: specify the database schema changes, describe the API webhook payload, calculate the LTV/CAC ratio, or define the precision-recall thresholds you would use to gauge model success.
